title: Qatar Loses $24 Billion as LNG Exports Collapse 96 Percent in Hormuz Crisis
excerpt: The Gulf state has exported just 18 LNG cargoes in six months, down from 509 a year earlier, while damage to the Ras Laffan complex could take five years to repair.
body:
• Qatar has lost $24 billion in LNG revenue over six months — roughly five months of national income — as the Hormuz crisis slashed exports by 96%
  • Only 18 LNG cargoes have left Qatar since the war began, down from 509 in the same period last year, according to data firm ICIS
  • Iranian drone and missile strikes damaged Qatar's Ras Laffan complex, the world's largest LNG facility, which could take five years and $20 billion per year to repair
  • European gas storage has fallen to a historic low for the time of year, with Goldman Sachs warning prices must jump by December to build adequate winter inventory

Six months into the U.S.-Iran war, Qatar has emerged as the conflict's single biggest energy casualty, with liquefied natural gas exports collapsing by 96% and the Gulf state hemorrhaging an estimated $24 billion in lost revenue, Reuters calculations show.

The figure represents roughly five months of national income based on 2025 data, a staggering blow to an economy that derived much of its wealth from being the world's second-largest LNG exporter before the war.

From 509 Cargoes to 18

The numbers tell a stark story. Qatar managed to export just 18 LNG cargoes since the conflict began in late February, compared with 509 in the same period a year earlier, according to data intelligence firm ICIS. Two Qatari tankers have been attacked during transit through the Strait of Hormuz.

While neighboring Gulf oil exporters — Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Iraq, and Kuwait — have seen their exports disrupted, none has suffered anything close to Qatar's proportional loss. Oil exporters have managed to sneak cargoes secretly through the strait; LNG tankers, far larger and harder to conceal, have not.

State-owned QatarEnergy did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Ras Laffan: $20 Billion a Year in Damage

Beyond the blockade, Iranian drone and missile strikes have directly damaged Qatar's Ras Laffan industrial complex, the single largest LNG-producing facility on earth. QatarEnergy estimates the damage will cost approximately $20 billion per year in lost production capacity and could take up to five years to fully repair.

The company has been forced to declare force majeure for up to five years on some long-term LNG supply contracts — an extraordinary move that has rippled through global energy markets and thrown into question the reliability of Gulf-sourced LNG for years to come.

U.S. Producers Fill the Gap

Before the war, Qatar supplied approximately one-fifth of global daily LNG volumes. The vacuum has created a windfall for U.S. LNG exporters, who have ramped up deliveries to Asia and Europe. American producers have signed 10 new deals totaling 7.27 million tonnes annually since the conflict began, with Venture Global accounting for six of those agreements.

Total U.S. LNG exports have risen year-over-year as new export terminals have come online, accelerating a structural shift in global gas trade that may outlast the conflict itself.

Europe Faces a Cold Winter

The collapse in Qatari supply has hit Europe particularly hard. Gas storage levels across the continent have fallen to a historic low for the time of year, exposing the region to severe price spikes if the coming winter is cold.

Goldman Sachs warned earlier this month that European natural gas prices need to rise significantly by December for storage facilities to fill adequately — a scenario that would compound the energy-driven inflation already building across the continent. Asian and European gas prices have surged to three-year highs.

The de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz has trapped roughly 20% of daily global LNG flows, creating what energy analysts describe as the most sustained disruption to global gas markets since the energy crises of the 1970s. With Ras Laffan's repair timeline measured in years rather than months, the reshaping of global LNG trade routes may prove permanent.
